title: Decomposition and abstraction
explanation: Decomposition breaks a large problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Abstraction removes unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters for solving the problem, e.g. a bus map shows routes but not exact road shapes.

title: Flowcharts and pseudocode
explanation: Flowcharts represent an algorithm visually using standard shapes for start/end, process steps, and decisions. Pseudocode expresses the same logic in structured, plain-English-like statements, independent of any real language.

title: Searching and sorting algorithms
explanation: Linear search checks items one by one: it works on unsorted data but is slow. Binary search halves a sorted list each step, which is much faster. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order items to sort a list, at the cost of being slow on large lists. Merge sort splits the list in half repeatedly, then merges the sorted halves back together, which is much faster on large lists.

title: Trace tables and types of error
explanation: A trace table records the value of each variable at every step of an algorithm, so you can work out its output or spot where it goes wrong. There are three types of error: syntax errors (the code breaks the rules of the language), logic errors (the program runs but gives the wrong result) and runtime errors (the program crashes while running, e.g. dividing by zero).

title: Truth tables and logical operators
explanation: A truth table lists every combination of inputs to a logic expression and the output for each. The logical operators are AND (true only if both inputs are true), OR (true if at least one input is true) and NOT (flips the input). Truth tables can have up to three inputs, which gives 8 rows (2 x 2 x 2).

title: Binary and hexadecimal representation
explanation: Computers store everything as binary (0s and 1s). Hexadecimal is a compact way for humans to read binary, since each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.

title: Two's complement, binary addition, shifts and overflow
explanation: Unsigned integers use every bit for the value (8 bits holds 0 to 255). Two's complement lets the same bits hold negative numbers: with 8 bits the range is -128 to +127. Binary addition follows column rules (1 + 1 = 10, carrying the 1). A logical shift moves the bits left or right, filling gaps with 0s; a left shift doubles the number and a right shift halves it. An arithmetic shift keeps the sign bit so it works on two's complement numbers. Overflow happens when the result is too big for the bits available.

title: Units of data storage
explanation: Data is measured in bits and bytes (8 bits), scaling up through kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes, each roughly 1000 times the size of the previous unit.

title: Character sets and image representation
explanation: Character sets like ASCII and Unicode assign a unique number to every character a computer can display. A bitmap image is stored as a grid of pixels, where each pixel's colour is a binary value; more bits per pixel (colour depth) allows more colours, and resolution is the number of pixels.

title: Representing sound
explanation: Analogue sound is converted to binary by sampling: measuring the amplitude (height) of the sound wave at regular intervals. The sample rate is how many samples are taken per second, the sample interval is the time between samples, and the bit depth is how many bits are used for each sample. A higher sample rate and bit depth give better quality but a larger file.

title: Data compression
explanation: Compression makes files smaller. Lossless compression removes redundancy so the file can be perfectly restored; lossy compression permanently discards some detail for greater size savings (common for images, audio and video).

title: The von Neumann concept and the CPU
explanation: In the von Neumann stored program concept, program instructions and data are both held in main memory (RAM), and the CPU fetches each instruction, decodes it and executes it, repeating continuously (the fetch-decode-execute cycle). The CPU contains the control unit (directs the cycle), the arithmetic logic unit (ALU, does calculations and logic) and registers (tiny, very fast storage), and is paced by the clock. Three buses link the CPU and memory: the address bus (carries the memory address to use), the data bus (carries data and instructions) and the control bus (carries control signals such as read or write).

title: Secondary storage: magnetic, optical and solid state
explanation: Secondary storage keeps data permanently, even when the power is off. Magnetic storage (hard disk drives) stores data as magnetised patterns on a surface: it is cheap per gigabyte with large capacity, but slower and has moving parts. Optical storage (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) uses a laser to read a disc: it is cheap and portable but has low capacity and is slow. Solid state storage (SSDs, USB sticks, memory cards) uses electronic circuits with no moving parts: it is fast, silent and durable but costs more per gigabyte.

title: Embedded systems
explanation: An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to perform a dedicated task, e.g. a microwave, washing machine or a car's engine management system. It usually runs one fixed program and has limited memory and processing power.

title: Software: system vs application
explanation: System software (like the operating system) manages the computer itself: memory, processes, peripherals. Application software (like a word processor or web browser) lets the user perform specific tasks.

title: Operating system and utility software
explanation: An operating system provides file management (organising files and folders), process management (running and switching between programs), peripheral management (controlling devices) and user management (accounts, passwords and permissions). Utility software looks after the system, for example file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation and anti-malware.

title: Developing robust software
explanation: Robust software copes with unexpected input and problems without failing. Vulnerabilities can be identified using audit trails (a record of who did what and when) and code reviews (other people checking the code for mistakes and security holes).

title: Low-level and high-level languages
explanation: Low-level languages (machine code and assembly language) are close to the hardware: they run fast and give precise control, but they are hard to write and tied to a particular type of processor. High-level languages (like Python) are easier to read and write and work on many machines, but must be translated into machine code before they run.

title: Interpreters and compilers
explanation: A compiler translates the whole high-level program into machine code before it runs, producing a fast program that can be run again without the source code. An interpreter translates and runs the program one line at a time, which makes finding errors easier, but the program runs more slowly and needs the interpreter each time.

title: Network types: LAN and WAN
explanation: Computers are connected in a network so they can share resources (files, printers, an internet connection) and communicate. A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small local area, e.g. one school. A WAN (Wide Area Network) spans a wider area, often using third-party infrastructure like the internet.

title: Network topologies: bus, star and mesh
explanation: A topology is the way devices on a network are arranged. In a bus topology all devices share one main cable: it is cheap and simple, but a break in the cable stops the network and heavy traffic slows it. In a star topology every device connects to a central switch: a failed cable only affects one device, but if the switch fails the whole network goes down. In a mesh topology devices connect directly to several others: there are many routes so it keeps working if a link fails, but it needs a lot of cabling and costs more.

title: Wired and wireless connections and network speed
explanation: Wired connections (e.g. Ethernet cables) are usually faster, more reliable and more secure. Wireless connections (e.g. Wi-Fi) are convenient and allow movement but have limited range and can suffer interference. Performance depends on speed, range, latency (the delay before data arrives) and bandwidth (how much data can be sent per second). Network speed is measured in bits per second (kilobit, megabit, gigabit), and transfer time = file size in bits divided by transmission rate in bits per second.

title: The internet and protocols
explanation: The internet is a global network of networks. Devices are identified by IP addresses and routers forward data between networks. Protocols are agreed rules for communication: Ethernet (wired networks), Wi-Fi (wireless networks), TCP/IP (breaks data into packets and routes them), HTTP and HTTPS (web pages, with HTTPS adding encryption) and FTP (file transfer). Email uses SMTP to send, and POP3 or IMAP to receive: POP3 downloads messages to your device, while IMAP keeps them on the server so several devices can see them.

title: The 4-layer TCP/IP model
explanation: The TCP/IP model has four layers. The application layer is where network applications such as web browsers and email programs operate. The transport layer sets up communication between the two hosts and agrees settings such as the size of packets. The internet layer addresses and packages data for transmission and routes the packets across the network. The link layer is where the network hardware, such as the network interface card, is located.

title: Network security: finding and preventing vulnerabilities
explanation: Networks hold sensitive data, so protecting them matters. Vulnerabilities can be found by penetration testing (authorised testers try to break in) and ethical hacking. Networks are protected by access control (user accounts, passwords and permissions), physical security (locked rooms, door locks) and firewalls (which block unauthorised traffic).

title: Environmental impacts of digital devices
explanation: Digital devices affect the environment through energy consumption (running devices and data centres), manufacture (raw materials and pollution), the replacement cycle (people upgrading often) and disposal (electronic waste containing harmful materials).

title: Personal data: legal and ethical issues
explanation: Collecting and using personal data raises issues of privacy, ownership, consent, misuse and data protection. In the UK, the Data Protection Act and UK GDPR set rules for how personal data must be handled.

title: AI, machine learning and robotics
explanation: Using artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotics raises ethical and legal questions: accountability (who is responsible when it gets something wrong?), safety, algorithmic bias (unfair results, often caused by biased training data) and legal liability.

title: Protecting intellectual property
explanation: Computer systems and software can be protected by copyright (automatically protects original work such as code), patents (protect inventions), trademarks (protect brand names and logos) and licensing (rules about how others may use the software).

title: Cybersecurity threats
explanation: Malware is software designed to cause harm: viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and key loggers. Hackers exploit technical vulnerabilities such as unpatched software and out-of-date anti-malware, and use social engineering such as phishing (tricking users into revealing information). Brute-force attacks try many passwords automatically, and SQL injection crafts input to manipulate a database query. The Computer Misuse Act makes unauthorised access to computer systems illegal.
code:
-- Never build a query by concatenating raw user input:
-- "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'"
-- Use a parameterised query instead, so input can't change the query's structure
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?;

title: Protecting digital systems and data
explanation: Digital systems and data can be protected using anti-malware software, encryption (scrambling data so it can't be read without a key), acceptable use policies (rules on how a system may be used), and backup and recovery procedures (copies of data kept safely so it can be restored after loss or an attack).

title: Sequence, selection and iteration
explanation: Every program combines three constructs: sequence (steps run in order), selection (if/elif/else to branch), and iteration (for/while to repeat).

title: Variables, constants and data types
explanation: A variable's value can change while a program runs; a constant is fixed. Core data types: integer, real/float, Boolean, character, and string.
code:
PI = 3.14159          # constant (by convention, not enforced)
radius = 4             # variable
area = PI * radius ** 2
print(area)

title: Arrays (1D and 2D)
explanation: A 1D array (Python list) stores an ordered sequence of values accessed by a single index. A 2D array stores values in a grid, accessed with a row and column index, which is useful for tables or game boards.

title: String handling
explanation: Strings can be sliced, searched, and transformed using built-in operations: getting length, changing case, extracting substrings, and joining/splitting.

title: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators
explanation: Arithmetic operators do calculations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus (the remainder), integer division and exponentiation (powers). Relational operators compare values: equal to, not equal to, less than, greater than, less than or equal to and greater than or equal to. Logical operators combine conditions: AND, OR and NOT.
code:
print(17 // 5)   # 3  (integer division)
print(17 % 5)    # 2  (modulus)
print(2 ** 8)    # 256 (exponentiation)
print(7 >= 7)    # True
print(True and not False)  # True

title: Subprograms: functions and procedures
explanation: Breaking a program into subprograms makes it easier to read, test, and reuse. A function returns a value to the caller; a procedure carries out actions without necessarily returning one.

title: Input validation and testing
explanation: Validation rejects clearly wrong input before it's used. Common checks are a length check, a presence check, a range check (e.g. a mark between 0 and 100) and a pattern check. Authentication confirms who a user is, for example with an ID and password or a lookup. Testing a program should use normal, boundary, and erroneous data to confirm it behaves correctly in every case.

title: Reading and writing CSV files
explanation: A CSV (comma separated values) text file stores a table of data with one row per line and the values separated by commas. Programs can write rows to a CSV file to save data and read them back later.
code:
import csv

with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Alex", 72])
    writer.writerow(["Sam", 85])

with open("marks.csv") as f:
    for name, mark in csv.reader(f):
        print(name, mark)

title: Writing readable programs
explanation: Programs are easier to read, understand and maintain when they use good layout, indentation, comments, meaningful identifiers (names that say what a variable or subprogram is for) and white space.
